submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on a subword continuation fragment - a token with no leading space, i.e. the model is in the middle of spelling out a word - when that word is not ordinary English vocabulary: a foreign or non-English name, a place name, or a Greco-Latin technical or loan word (hyp|od|ermic, Bh|ut|to, immunoglob|ul|ins, ang|ust|ifolia, Sand|i|k, gluc|oc|orticoids, har|ic|ot). It fires roughly nine times more often on mid-word fragments than on a word's first token (0.8% vs 0.09% of scanned tokens, and only 9 of the top 100 peaks are word-initial), and goes silent when the fragment is preceded by a space or when the word is an equally long everyday English word (photo|synthesis, mito|chond|ria, under|standing, tomo|graphy).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: On the morning of the inspection the head of conservation unlocked the east gallery and led the visitors past a row of packing crates. She explained that the museum had spent three years negotiating the loan, and that every object in the room had travelled by lorry from a storeroom outside the city. The group stopped in front of a display case where a technician was adjusting a light meter. Dust, she said, was the enemy; the filters in the ceiling had to be changed every six weeks, and the humidity had to stay steady right through the summer. A curator from the antiquities department described how the collection had been assembled in the nineteen twenties by a wealthy shipping family, and how most of the records had been lost during the war. For years nobody knew where half the pieces had come from. Then a student matched the inventory numbers to a ledger in the national archive, and the history of the whole group became clear. The visitors moved on to a smaller room, where a row of painted panels hung behind glass. The colours had faded unevenly, the curator said, because the panels had once faced a window. Conservators had spent months removing a yellowed varnish with swabs and a mild solvent, working under a microscope one square centimetre at a time. In the corridor a young woman in a white coat explained the loan agreement and the insurance schedule, and answered questions about the temperature in the storeroom. Someone asked whether the public would be allowed to watch the work. Not yet, she said, but the museum hoped to open a window into the laboratory later in the year. The last room was colder than the others, and here the conservators were treating a group of Attic amphorae recovered from a shipwreck off the coast, lifting the salt crust from the clay with a fine brush while the smell of the solvent hung in the air. Outside, the delegation waited for their cars in the courtyard, and the head of conservation said that the work would take another five years at least.
